name: Homomorphic Encryption
description: Homomorphic encryption allows computation on encrypted data without decrypting it first, producing encrypted results that, when decrypted, match the results of performing the same operations on the plaintext. This enables secure outsourced computation where sensitive data remains encrypted throughout processing. By allowing ML operations on encrypted data, it provides strong privacy guarantees for applications involving highly sensitive information.

name: Algorithm Review Boards
description: An algorithm review board is a standing, multidisciplinary body inside an organisation that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects at set points and decides whether, and on what conditions, they may proceed. The literature also calls these bodies AI ethics boards or AI review boards. They differ from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because they also weigh harms to the people a system will affect and to society. A risk-based triage decides which projects need full review; the project team then submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, and members drawn from technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds, sometimes with people from affected communities, question the team and iterate on that account with them. The board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects, and the output is a dated decision record with its reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built.

name: Red Teaming
description: Red teaming is a structured adversarial evaluation process in which a dedicated team systematically probes an AI/ML system to discover vulnerabilities and failure modes. Unlike individual testing techniques (such as prompt injection testing, jailbreak resistance testing, or safety envelope testing), red teaming defines the organisational methodology: team composition, campaign planning, attack taxonomy, and reporting structure. The red team coordinates diverse attack vectors — including prompt manipulation, adversarial examples, edge case exploitation, and social engineering scenarios — into a coherent assessment programme. Results feed into risk registers and remediation plans rather than pass/fail metrics.

name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards establish systematic checkpoints where human experts review, validate, or override AI/ML system decisions before they take effect. This governance approach combines automated efficiency with human judgement by defining clear intervention criteria (such as uncertainty thresholds, risk levels, or sensitive contexts) that trigger mandatory human oversight. By incorporating domain expertise, ethical considerations, and contextual understanding that machines may lack, these safeguards help ensure that critical decisions maintain appropriate human accountability whilst preserving the benefits of automated processing for routine cases.

name: Confidence Thresholding
description: Confidence thresholding creates decision boundaries based on model uncertainty scores, routing predictions into different handling workflows depending on their confidence levels. High-confidence predictions (e.g., above 95%) proceed automatically, whilst medium-confidence cases (e.g., 70-95%) may trigger additional validation or human review, and low-confidence predictions (below 70%) receive extensive oversight or default to conservative fallback actions. This technique enables organisations to maintain automated efficiency for clear-cut cases whilst ensuring appropriate human intervention for uncertain decisions, balancing operational speed with risk management across safety-critical applications.

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers watch a deployed AI system's operational and model-level signals and automatically stop, limit or reroute calls to the model when those signals cross preset limits. The circuit breaker, a software resilience pattern, wraps calls to the model: while closed it passes requests through and counts failures in a rolling time window; when failures pass a threshold it opens, so further requests fail at once or receive a fallback such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person; after a cooldown it half-opens and lets a few trial requests through, closing again only if they succeed. For a machine learning model, what counts as a failure is widened from errors and timeouts to model-level signals available at the moment of prediction, such as input drift scores, low prediction confidence, out-of-range outputs or limits on the actions the system may take, because true accuracy usually cannot be measured until outcomes arrive later. The output is a log of breaker state changes, the metrics that triggered them and the alerts raised, which shows when and why the system was restricted; the protection is only as good as the chosen thresholds and the fallback behind the breaker.

name: Data Poisoning Detection
description: Data poisoning detection identifies malicious training data designed to compromise model behaviour. This technique detects various poisoning attacks including backdoor injection (triggers causing specific behaviours), availability attacks (degrading overall performance), and targeted attacks (causing errors on specific inputs). Detection methods include statistical outlier analysis, influence function analysis to identify high-impact training points, and validation-based approaches that test for suspicious model behaviours indicative of poisoning.

name: Model Extraction Defence Testing
description: Model extraction defence testing evaluates protections against attackers who attempt to steal model functionality by querying it and training surrogate models. This technique assesses defences like query limiting, output perturbation, watermarking, and fingerprinting by simulating extraction attacks and measuring how much model functionality can be replicated. Testing evaluates both the effectiveness of defences in preventing extraction and their impact on legitimate use cases, ensuring security measures don't excessively degrade user experience.

name: Membership Inference Attack Testing
description: Membership inference attack testing evaluates whether adversaries can determine if specific data points were included in a model's training set. This technique simulates attacks where adversaries use model confidence scores, prediction patterns, or loss values to distinguish training data from non-training data. Testing measures privacy leakage by calculating attack success rates, precision-recall trade-offs, and advantage over random guessing. Results inform decisions about privacy-enhancing techniques like differential privacy or regularisation.

name: Trigger-Set Model Watermarking
description: Trigger-set model watermarking lets the owner of a trained classifier show later that a suspect model was copied from theirs, by planting a secret behaviour that only the owner can demonstrate. Before release, the owner chooses a small secret trigger set (in the originating scheme, 100 abstract images), gives each input a label the model would not otherwise predict, and trains or fine-tunes the model to return those labels while keeping its accuracy on the real task. In the originating scheme the owner also records cryptographic commitments to the trigger inputs and their labels, which fix the watermark at release so that a trigger set cannot be invented once a dispute has begun. To verify, the owner, or an arbiter shown the opened commitments, sends the trigger inputs to the suspect model through its ordinary prediction interface and counts how many return the assigned labels; an independently trained model matches them at about chance level, so a match rate above a preset threshold is evidence of copying. The technique produces the watermarked model, the commitments and, for each verification, the suspect model's trigger-set accuracy against the threshold.

name: Prompt Injection Testing
description: Prompt injection testing systematically evaluates LLMs and generative AI systems for vulnerabilities where malicious users can override system instructions through carefully crafted inputs. This technique encompasses both offensive security testing (proactively attempting injection attacks to identify vulnerabilities) and defensive detection mechanisms (monitoring for suspicious patterns in prompts and context). Testing involves evaluating various injection patterns including direct instruction manipulation, context confusion, role-playing exploits, delimiter attacks, and context window poisoning. Detection methods analyse context provenance, validate formatting consistency, and identify semantic anomalies that indicate manipulation attempts rather than legitimate user interaction.
